common_name: The Prince Rose (Deep Crimson-Purple David Austin Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; The Prince is a compact David Austin rose whose deep crimson blooms age toward purple as they open.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost. Introduced by David Austin in 1990, The Prince bears very deep crimson-red, densely petaled, rosette-shaped blooms that darken toward a rich purple-maroon as they age, one of the deepest, most saturated flower colors in the English rose line, carrying a strong old-rose fragrance. Its compact, bushy habit fits smaller beds and containers better than many larger-growing Austin roses. It reblooms in flushes from late spring through fall; prune canes back by about a third in late winter to encourage strong new flowering wood, and provide good air circulation to help manage black spot in humid conditions.
sources: American Rose Society — English rose archive

common_name: Wenlock Rose (Deep Red David Austin Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun with good air circulation; Wenlock bears rich deep red, rosette-shaped blooms on an upright, vigorous shrub.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost. Introduced by David Austin in 1994, Wenlock bears deep crimson-red, fully double, rosette-shaped blooms with a moderate old-rose fragrance on a vigorous, upright shrub that holds its color well without the fading toward purple seen in some other dark red English roses. It reblooms in flushes from late spring through fall, and its strong, upright growth habit makes it useful toward the back of a mixed border or as a hedge element among other roses. Prune canes back by about a third in late winter, deadhead spent blooms through the season, and provide good air circulation to help keep foliage clean.
sources: American Rose Society — English rose archive

common_name: Golden Wings Rose (Large Single Pale Yellow Cold-Hardy Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun to light shade in well-drained, fertile soil; Golden Wings is exceptionally cold-hardy and disease-resistant for a rose with such large flowers.

directions: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in well-drained, fertile soil. Golden Wings, introduced in 1956, bears extra-large single flowers — some of the biggest single blooms of any commonly grown rose — in a soft, pale primrose-yellow with prominent amber stamens, opening over an unusually long bloom season from late spring through fall. Its combination of exceptional cold hardiness, strong disease resistance, and near-continuous bloom has made it one of the most consistently recommended shrub roses by rose experts for decades, thriving with far less spray intervention than most roses of its era require. The open, single flower form is also especially valuable to pollinators, which can access the stamens easily. Prune lightly in late winter to shape the rounded, bushy shrub and remove dead or crossing wood.

common_name: Sally Holmes Rose (Large-Clustered Ivory-to-Pink Shrub Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root or container plants in spring or fall in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil; Sally Holmes grows tall and can be trained as a short climber against a wall or fence, or left to form a large freestanding shrub.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil. Sally Holmes, introduced in 1976, bears huge, hydrangea-like clusters of single to semi-double flowers that open ivory-white flushed with soft pink and age toward a deeper blush, an especially dramatic and long-lasting flower display for a shrub rose. It grows tall and vigorous, and can be pruned to stay as a large freestanding shrub or trained as a short climber against a wall, fence, or pillar. It reblooms reliably from late spring through fall and shows good disease resistance for an older cultivar. Prune to control size and shape in late winter, and deadhead spent clusters through the season to encourage continued flowering.
